0075.event: In Malawi, far south of the great Rift Valley, diggers found a fossil jawbone laid down about two million four hundred fifty thousand years ago. It belonged to one of the early tool-bearers, the same kind of folk who were striking sharp flakes from stone farther north. One jaw cannot tell a whole story, but it can tell a direction. It says these people were not staying put in a single valley. They were spreading, following water and game southward across open country. The southern frontier was never a line drawn on a map. It was walked into being, one camp at a time, by feet that kept going. Every new found bone pushes the boundary a little farther, and this one pushed it far.
0075.announce: A frontier tale in verse: The Southern Frontier.
0075.title: The Southern Frontier
0075.piece:
They found a jawbone south of the Rift,
where the lake spreads wide and the hills lift.
Two million years and more it lay,
while the tool-bearers walked away,
south and south, past valley and plain,
following water, following rain.
One jaw, one people, moving on,
from the old ground to the new dawn.
The frontier was not drawn, but done,
step by step, under the sun.
No flag, no fence, no claimed domain,
just feet, and hunger, and the plain.
The south was won the walking way,
and we are walking still today.

0076.event: In Tanzania, in the gorge country of Olduvai, diggers found the bones of a new kind of human laid down about two million four hundred thousand years ago. The brain was larger than anything before it, and the hands were built for gripping, with a thumb that could meet the fingers in a firm hold. This was Homo habilis, the handy man, and the hands explain the name. Stone tools lie scattered through the same layers, and the grip may be what made them possible. Strength still belonged to the lions. What belonged to the handy man was the pause before the blow, the small decision the mind makes before the hand moves. That pause is where we begin.
0076.announce: For the first toolmaker, a song: The Handy Man.
0076.title: The Handy Man
0076.piece:
Bigger brain and a gripping hand,
he rose up in the gorge land.
Thumb to finger, stone to stone,
he struck the flake and made it known.
Handy man, handy man,
hold the future in your hand.
Not the strongest, not the fleet,
but the mind made hands complete.
Every tool that we have made,
every blade and every spade,
started with that pause, that plan,
in the hand of the handy man.
Lions had the strength and pride.
He had the thought he held inside.
Stone by stone, and blow by blow,
he taught the hands the way to know.

0077.event: In Tanzania, beside the bones of the handy man, lie animal bones marked with fine cuts, laid down about two million three hundred thirty thousand years ago. The marks match stone flakes, and the pattern tells a plain story. The lions ate first, as lions do. Then the tool-bearers moved in and cut meat from what was left, cracking bones for the rich marrow inside. They were not hunters yet. They were not strong enough to bring down big game. But they were clever, and clever is a kind of strength. They ate meat when they could, and the fat fed their growing brains. There is no shame in the scavenger's trade. Somebody has to be second, and the second one with a sharp stone eats well.
0077.announce: A scavenger's ballad: The Skilled Scavenger.
0077.title: The Skilled Scavenger
0077.piece:
The lions ate their fill and moved away,
and left the bones upon the ground.
The tool-bearers came at close of day
and cut the meat they found.
They were not hunters, not yet strong,
but clever hands make do.
They cracked the bones both short and long
and ate the marrow through.
Rich fat for brains that needed more,
a feast from lion's leavings.
The scavenger's trade is never poor
when stone gives second helpings.

0078.event: In Kenya, on an old land surface laid down about two million three hundred thousand years ago, lies a scatter of stone cores and sharp flakes, hundreds of them, all struck in the same practiced way. Hands came back to this spot again and again, sat down, and made tools. It was an open-air workshop, the earliest known place set aside for making things. Someone had to teach and someone had to learn, because the flakes are too alike to be accident. They were swept aside, the good ones kept, and the work went on day after day. Two million years before the factory, we already had the idea: a place, a craft, and hands that return to it.
0078.announce: The workshop floor rings out in this verse: The Workshop Floor.
0078.title: The Workshop Floor
0078.piece:
Sit down. The stone is waiting here.
The core is set. The flakes fall near.
Strike true, strike clean, the edge is bright.
We make the tools by morning light.
This is the floor where work is done,
beneath the wide and watching sun.
No walls, no roof, no bell, no boss,
just hands, and stone, and gain, and loss.
The teacher shows. The learner tries.
The bad flake breaks. The good flake flies.
We sweep the waste and start anew.
There is always work for hands to do.
Come back tomorrow. Come back true.
The workshop floor is waiting for you.

0079.event: In South Africa, in the limestone caves of Sterkfontein, diggers freed a nearly perfect skull laid down about two million years ago. It belonged to Australopithecus africanus, the southern ape, and the finder nicknamed it Mrs. Ples, for Plesianthropus, the near-man. The skull is small-brained but beautifully formed, with a rounded dome and small teeth, and it may have belonged to a male despite the name. Names are our business, not theirs. What matters is the face itself, gazing out of the stone after two million years, proof that our family once lived and walked under the southern sun long before we were human.
0079.announce: A smiling poem for the lady of the limestone: Mrs. Ples.
0079.title: Mrs. Ples
0079.piece:
Out of the limestone, out of the deep,
where the dark caves their secrets keep,
she rises, smiling, round and fair,
two million years of patient air.
Mrs. Ples they called her, near to man,
though she may be he. We name as we can.
Small brain, small teeth, a graceful dome,
a face that made the stone its home.
She walked the south when we were young,
before a single song was sung.
I stand before her, and I bow.
We remember. We remember now.
The stone gave back what time had lent.
She smiles. She knows what smiling meant.

0080.event: In South Africa, in the cave deposits of Malapa, lie the bones of a young one laid down about one million nine hundred eighty thousand years ago. The brain was small, but the arms were long for climbing and the hands were shaped much like ours, built for gripping. Here was a creature living between worlds: at home in the trees and on the ground, climbing when the leopards prowled and walking when the way was clear. The young ones stayed close to the high branches, as young ones do. The hands that gripped the branches would one day grip the pen and the plow. But on that spring long ago, they only held on tight.
0080.announce: A lullaby for the climbing child: The Spring Child.
0080.title: The Spring Child
0080.piece:
Hush now, little climber, hold the branch,
the leopard walks below.
Your hands are shaped like ours to come,
and this is all you know.
Climb up high where the green leaves hide you,
swing where the tall trees grow.
Walk the ground when the sun is kind,
then climb again, soft and slow.
Small of brain and long of arm,
between the earth and sky,
you are the spring the world was waiting for,
the reason wonder asks why.
Sleep now, child, in the high green cradle.
The ancient world is wide.
The hands that hold the branch tonight
hold tomorrow deep inside.

0081.event: In Kenya, about one million nine hundred thousand years ago, a new kind of human appears in the fossil record. Homo erectus stood tall on long legs, narrow of body, built to walk and run under the equatorial sun. The climbing shoulders were gone. These were striders, made for the open country, and they would wander farther than any ancestor before them: out of Africa, across Asia, to the farthest shores. The brain was bigger, the stride was longer, and the horizon was wider. Everything that came after, including us, walks in the track of those long legs.
0081.announce: An anthem for the tall wanderers: The Rise of Erectus.
0081.title: The Rise of Erectus
0081.piece:
Stand up tall on the long, long road.
The world is wide and new.
Erectus rises, strong and bold,
and walks the whole earth through.
No more the crouch, no more the tree,
the open plain is home.
The long legs carry far and free
wherever feet may roam.
To Asia's woods, to northern snow,
the wanderers will go.
They do not know how far they go.
But we who follow know.
So lift your stride and walk the land.
The ancient road is true.
The tall ones walked it first of all.
Now it is walked by you.

0082.event: At Kanjera in Kenya, about one million eight hundred fifty thousand years ago, stone flakes lie beside the bones of whole antelope. The cut marks show the animals were butchered joint by joint, and the meat was carried, which means many hands shared the work. This may not have been scavenging leftovers. The band seems to have taken the kill and divided it, and everyone ate. The strong could have kept it all. They did not. Around that carcass, something new was happening besides dinner. The first butcher's knife cut more than meat. It cut the old rule that the strong eat and the weak wait. Sharing had begun, and sharing is a kind of promise.
0082.announce: A butcher's hymn in plain verse: The First Butcher's Knife.
0082.title: The First Butcher's Knife
0082.piece:
Lay the antelope on the ground.
Pass the flakes. Stand close around.
Cut the joint and share the meat.
Everyone eats. The meal is sweet.
The strong ones could have taken all.
It seems they did not. They heard the call
of the band, the shared demand:
no one hungry in this land.
The knife is sharp, the cut is clean,
the kindest thing the world has seen.
It cut the meat. It cut much more.
It cut the lock on hunger's door.
We carry for the ones too slow.
We share because we share, you know.
The blade divides. The love unites.
This is the first of human rites.

0083.event: In the Caucasus mountains of Georgia, at a place called Dmanisi, lie five skulls laid down about one million eight hundred thousand years ago. They belonged to small-brained wanderers, kin of the African erectus, and they mark the first known human steps out of Africa. Beyond the mountains lay cold country, thin food, and winters none of their ancestors had known. They went anyway, on foot, carrying nothing but each other. The gate of Dmanisi is not a triumph arch. It is a doorway walked through by people who could not know what waited, and went because going was what they did.
0083.announce: At the mountain gate, a marching song: The Gate of Dmanisi.
0083.title: The Gate of Dmanisi
0083.piece:
March through the gate where the mountains stand.
The cold wind calls beyond.
Leave the warm land, leave the known,
and walk the road beyond.
Five skulls to tell the tale we sing,
small-brained and brave and true.
They did not know what time would bring.
They walked. Now walk you too.
The snow was new. The night was long.
The food was thin and few.
But feet keep time with marching song,
and hearts keep marching through.
Dmanisi gate, we name you still,
the door the first walked past.
The human road runs over the hill,
and walking ever lasts.

0084.event: Among the Dmanisi skulls in Georgia is one that belonged to a very old individual, laid down about one million seven hundred eighty thousand years ago. Every tooth was gone long before death, the sockets healed smooth. Without teeth he could not chew, and without chewing he should have died. He did not die. Someone likely mashed his food soft, day after day, and fed him long after he could hunt or work or pay his way. This is the oldest known proof of care for the helpless. The first migrants crossed the mountains carrying more than tools. They carried love for one who could give nothing back.
0084.announce: An old man's elegy: The Toothless Old Man.
0084.title: The Toothless Old Man
0084.piece:
No teeth remained to chew the meat,
the years had worn them all away.
By every law he should have died.
He lived. Love found a way.
Someone, it seems, mashed the food soft and warm.
Someone brought it day by day.
Someone sat beside the old, old man
and would not go away.
He could not hunt. He could not run.
He gave no labor back.
But they carried him across the hills,
along the mountain track.
This is the first true human thing,
not tool, nor fire, nor art.
The toothless old man, fed and loved:
the proof of the human heart.

0085.event: At Kokiselei in Kenya, about one million seven hundred sixty thousand years ago, someone picked up a stone and shaped it on both faces into a teardrop blade with a sharp edge all around. It was the first handaxe, and it was more than a tool. It was symmetrical, planned, and beautiful, the same shape made again and again for over a million years, because it could hardly be improved. The maker had to hold the finished form in mind before the first strike. That is the difference between breaking a stone and making a thing. Some call the handaxe the oldest art on earth. They may be right.
0085.announce: A maker's hymn for the first blade: The Handaxe Is Born.
0085.title: The Handaxe Is Born
0085.piece:
Take the stone in your knowing hand.
See the blade it hides inside.
Strike one face, then turn, then strike,
let the waste fall open wide.
Both sides shaped, the edge runs true,
a teardrop, keen and plain.
A million years will honor you.
The form will long remain.
Not broken rock, but born design,
held in the mind before the blow.
The oldest art is in this line,
the first true thing we know.
Lift up the handaxe to the sun.
No words need to be said.
The maker knew when it was done.
The blade was born, not bred.

0086.event: In the Olduvai Gorge of Tanzania, about one million seven hundred fifty thousand years ago, two tool traditions lie side by side in the same layers. There are the simple choppers and flakes of the old way, and beside them the new shaped handaxes, symmetrical and planned. It is as if two peoples shared the gorge, or as if one people were learning a new answer while keeping the old. Did they trade ideas, or keep to their own fires? The stones do not say. But the gorge held both, and the water and shade were shared. Difference is older than we think, and the valley was wide enough for two truths at once.
0086.announce: Two stones, two peoples, one verse: Two Kinds of Stone.
0086.title: Two Kinds of Stone
0086.piece:
Two kinds of stone in the gorge today,
the chopper old, the handaxe new.
Two kinds of hands at work and play,
two kinds of minds to see it through.
Did they meet beside the stream?
Did they trade a look, a word?
Did they share the fire's gleam,
or pass like passing bird?
The gorge is wide. The water's shared.
The shade falls soft on all.
Two answers, and the valley cared
for each, both great and small.
So let the old and new lie near.
No need to choose, no need to fight.
Two kinds of stone are lying here,
and both of them are right.

0087.event: In Kenya, about one million seven hundred thousand years ago, the bodies of Homo erectus had grown tall and narrow, built to shed heat under the equatorial sun. They may have run down prey not by speed but by endurance, trotting for miles until the animal overheated and stopped. The body itself was the weapon: sweat glands, springy legs, and breath that would not quit. Anyone who has run long distances knows the strange joy that comes in the later miles. It is ancient. The long-legged runners felt it first, under a sun that never relented, and every runner since has felt their ghost in the chase.
0087.announce: A runner's chant for the long chase: The Long-Legged Runner.
0087.title: The Long-Legged Runner
0087.piece:
Run, run, the long, long run,
beneath the burning sun.
Not the fastest, but the last,
we run till the race is won.
Tall and narrow, built for heat,
we trot the miles away.
Perhaps the antelope knew defeat
before the close of day.
Sweat and breath and steady stride,
we do not stop, we stay.
The prey may falter, turn aside,
and we may win the day.
So run the miles the ancients ran.
The joy is deep and true.
The long-legged runner lives in man.
The runner lives in you.

0088.event: In Ethiopia, in the dry country of the Horn of Africa, lies a heavy-browed skull laid down about one million seven hundred thousand years ago. It belonged to Homo erectus, spreading through hot and open land where water was scarce and the sun showed no mercy. The thick brow shades the eyes like a built-in sunshade, and the strong bone speaks of a hard life met with hard answers. These were the ones who stayed and learned the dry places: where the water holes were, how long to wait, when to move on. The Horn always deals hardness. They answered it, and they lasted.
0088.announce: A desert verse for the heavy brow: The Daka Brow.
0088.title: The Daka Brow
0088.piece:
Beneath the heavy brow, the eyes
look out across the burning plain.
The Horn deals drought beneath hard skies,
and life is earned through pain.
Thick skull and bone, a patient mind,
that learned the water's way.
The ones who stay are the ones who find
their path through the hard day.
No easy valley, no soft rain,
just sun and wind and thirst.
But they who learn the dry plain
outlast it at its worst.
They chose to stay. They chose to learn.
They made the hard land home.
The Daka brow still looks our way,
wherever we may roam.

0089.event: In Kenya, about one million six hundred fifty thousand years ago, a scatter of animal bones, stone tools, and trampled earth marks a place the band returned to again and again. There were no walls and no roof, only a patch of shade and the familiar ground. But they came back, carrying meat and stone to this one spot, and that is what makes it feel like a home. Home was never the walls. Home was the return. Long before fire was tamed, before doors and hearths, the band had an address: here, this site, the place we always come back to. We have been coming back ever since.
0089.announce: A homecoming song for the first campsite: The Home Base.
0089.title: The Home Base
0089.piece:
Come back, come back, the day is done.
The shade is cool and deep.
The home base waits for everyone.
Come home to rest and sleep.
No walls of stone, no roof of thatch,
just earth we know so well.
The band comes back, the hearts attach
to the place the stories tell.
We carry meat. We carry stone.
We lay them on the ground.
This patch of earth is ours alone.
Here is where we're found.
Home is not the wall or door.
Home is the return.
We came back then, forevermore.
The home base holds us firm.

0090.event: By the shores of Lake Turkana in Kenya, diggers raised the nearly complete skeleton of a boy who died about one million six hundred thousand years ago, at roughly twelve years old. He was tall and strong for his age, with long legs built for distance, a young Homo erectus already shaped for the long walk. We do not know why he died so young. The bones keep that secret. But the legs tell the rest: he was made to greet the dawn in new country, season after season. Twelve years old, and already a traveler. The boy by the lake walked farther in his short life than most of us walk in ours.
0090.announce: A boy's marching verse: The Turkana Boy.
0090.title: The Turkana Boy
0090.piece:
Twelve years old by the waterside,
tall and straight and strong.
The Turkana Boy walked far and wide.
His stride was deep and long.
We do not know why he had to die.
The bones will never tell.
But he had walked beneath the sky,
and he had walked it well.
So rest now, traveler, rest your feet.
Your road runs ever on.
For every wanderer you meet
walks where your feet have gone.

0091.event: In Kenya, about one million five hundred fifty thousand years ago, the ground is littered with long bones smashed open with practiced blows. The band cracked every bone for the marrow inside, the rich fat that growing brains need most. It was not pretty work, but it was clever work. The best food was hidden where only a stone could reach it, and they knew exactly where to strike. They ate the gold inside and left the bare shafts scattered. We are, in a real sense, what we ate. Cracked bones and rich marrow fed the fire inside the skull, and the brain grew on the leavings of the kill.
0091.announce: A marrow feast, in a limerick: The Marrow Eaters.
0091.title: The Marrow Eaters
0091.piece:
There once was a band by the lake
who knew which bones were worth the break.
They smashed them with stones
for the fat in the bones.
The rich marrow was all they would take.
The lions ate first, as is right,
then they left in the soft morning light.
But the band with their stones
cracked the very best bones,
and they feasted till late in the night.

0092.event: In Kenya, about one million five hundred thousand years ago, footprints and scattered tools point east and north, toward the lands beyond Africa. The bands moved a night here, a season there, following game and water over the horizon. No one planned a migration. No leader pointed the way. They walked because walking was what they did, and the unknown kept pulling. The road was made by walking, and it is the oldest road there is. Every journey since, every ship and highway, is only a longer version of that first step east, taken because something beyond the hill might be better.
0092.announce: A road song for the outward path: The Outward Road.
0092.title: The Outward Road
0092.piece:
East and north, the footprints lead,
away from all we know.
The bands moved on at walking speed,
a night here, then they'd go.
No leader pointed out the way.
No map was ever drawn.
They followed game from day to day,
and walked toward the dawn.
The road was made by walking feet.
It is the oldest code.
The going calls, the hearts repeat:
step out upon the road.
So walk it now, the outward way,
the path the first ones trod.
Every road we walk today
began where they once stood.

0093.event: At Ileret in Kenya, about one million five hundred thousand years ago, two kinds of footprints cross the same ancient lakeshore mud. One set is large, the long stride of Homo erectus. The other is smaller, left by a cousin species walking the same shore close in time. They never met, as far as the mud can tell. Each passed unaware that another kind of human had walked there just before. The lake did not mind. There was water enough for all. For one brief span on one lakeshore, two kinds of humanity shared the same ground, and neither knew.
0093.announce: Footprints in mud, in a quiet verse: The Ileret Footprints.
0093.title: The Ileret Footprints
0093.piece:
Two trails in the lakeshore mud,
close in time, yet side by side.
The tall one walked, the small one stood
where the quiet waters glide.
Erectus strode with the long, long pace.
The cousin followed, light.
Perhaps they never saw each other's face.
They may have passed by day and night.
The mud kept only what feet could say.
The rest is lost to time.
But on that shore, so far away,
two human kinds walked in their prime.
The lake was wide. The water sweet.
There was enough for all.
Two kinds of human, on their feet,
both answered the same call.

0094.event: In Kenya, about one million four hundred fifty thousand years ago, the skulls of Homo erectus hold brain casts larger and rounder than before, shaped by minds that could plan ahead and hold tomorrow in thought. And with the bigger brain came something quieter. An elder could show a young one how to strike the stone, where the blow should fall, and the young one could watch and try again. No words were needed. Watch, try, fail, try again. The patience in those hands is older than language. Teaching is the first human art, older than any tool, and the lesson has never ended. We are still sitting in that circle, watching and trying.
0094.announce: A letter from the first teacher: The Teaching Hands.
0094.title: The Teaching Hands
0094.piece:
My child, sit down beside me here.
Watch my hands, and do not fear.
See how the stone is held just so.
Now strike. Let the bad flakes go.
Again. The angle was not right.
Watch once more in the morning light.
There. You felt it. That is true.
The stone has taught its craft to you.
No words we have, but hands can show
what patient hearts already know.
I learned this from my elder's hand,
as you will teach across the land.
The lesson has no final day.
We teach. We learn. We find the way.
So take the stone when I am gone,
and teach the young to carry on.
